1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. EMR: Elastic MapReduce; JDBC: Java Database Connectivity; ODBC: Open Database Connectivity; DPU: data processing unit; EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service; HDFS: Hadoop Distributed File System; TSV: tab-separated values; ORC: Optimized Row Columnar; VPC: Virtual Private Cloud; NAT: network address translation; VPN: virtual private network; BI: business intelligence; ECS: Elastic Container Service; ECR: Elastic Container Registry; SSL: Secure Sockets Layer; IAM: Identity and Access Management; REST: representational state transfer; SDK: software development kit; MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; RDS: Relational Database Service; AI: artificial intelligence; ML: machine learning; EBS: Elastic Block Store; OOM: out of memory; AQE: adaptive query execution

  • Choose the transformation service that fits a requirement: AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, AWS Lambda, Amazon Redshift, Athena
  • Convert formats (for example CSV to Apache Parquet) and know why
  • Connect to data sources with JDBC and ODBC and integrate several sources
  • Optimize cost and container usage while processing
  • Troubleshoot common transformation failures and slow jobs
  • Publish data through APIs and describe volume, velocity and variety
  • Use large language models (LLMs) inside data processing

2Choosing the Transformation Service (skill 1.2.5)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Cleans Its Data

  • Nightly order CSV files have mixed date formats and duplicates
  • Truck telemetry needs a join with the vehicle register held in a database
  • Analysts want Parquet files that Athena can scan cheaply
  • A delivery notes field holds free text that someone must classify
  • Your job: pick the right engine for each step

Service Best for Remember
AWS Glue Serverless Apache Spark ETL (and Python shell) with the Data Catalog, crawlers, bookmarks, workflows Pay for DPUs while jobs run; no clusters to manage; Flex execution for non-urgent jobs
Amazon EMR Big data frameworks (Spark, Hive, Presto, Flink, HBase) with full control of versions, libraries and tuning EMR on EC2 (clusters), EMR on EKS, EMR Serverless; Spot instances cut cost; transient clusters for batch
AWS Lambda Small, event-driven transformations (one file, one record batch) 15-minute limit, memory-bound; great for glue code and light ETL
Amazon Redshift SQL transformations inside the warehouse (ELT): INSERT ... SELECT, materialized views, stored procedures Data is loaded first, transformed in place
Amazon Athena SQL ETL on S3 with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) and INSERT INTO Serverless, pay per data scanned
AWS Glue DataBrew Visual, no-code cleaning and preparation (250+ transforms) For analysts, with profiling and recipes
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Stateful stream processing Module 2

Glue facts to know

  • A DPU (data processing unit) is 4 vCPU and 16 GB of memory; worker types include G.1X (1 DPU), G.2X (2), G.4X (4), G.8X (8) and memory-optimized R types; G.025X is only for low-volume streaming jobs [Verify live]
  • Job types: Spark (batch), Spark Streaming, Python shell (small jobs, no Spark)
  • Retries: 0 to 10 automatic restarts; timeouts are not retried. Maximum concurrency defaults to 1 run of the same job
  • Flex execution (jobs on Glue 3.0 or later with G.1X or G.2X workers) is cheaper and for non-urgent work (testing, one-time loads); standard execution is for time-sensitive work
  • Job run queuing lets runs wait instead of failing when quotas are hit
  • Glue Data Catalog as Hive metastore lets Spark, EMR and Athena share table definitions

EMR facts to know

  • Amazon EMR (formerly Elastic MapReduce) is a managed cluster platform for Hadoop, Spark and related tools
  • Node types: primary (coordinates), core (HDFS storage and tasks), task (compute only, ideal for Spot)
  • EMR Serverless: pick a runtime (Spark or Hive), submit jobs, and it scales workers automatically and releases them; pre-initialized capacity keeps workers warm for fast starts
  • Use S3 (EMRFS) for durable data and transient clusters that stop when the job ends
Exam tip

"Serverless, minimal operations, ETL with a catalog" → Glue. "Need a specific Spark/Hive version, custom libraries or Hadoop ecosystem tools" → EMR. "Occasional small transformation when a file arrives" → Lambda.

3File Formats and Conversion (skill 1.2.6)

Format Layout Use it for
CSV, TSV Row, text Exchange and simple loads; no schema, no types; large files are split only if uncompressed
JSON Row, text, semi-structured APIs and logs; nested data; verbose
Avro Row, binary, schema embedded Streaming and schema evolution (Kafka, Kinesis)
Apache Parquet Columnar, binary Analytics: Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, Glue; best default for the lake
Apache ORC Columnar, binary Hive-oriented analytics; often smaller files; richer complex types
  • Columnar formats compress by column, support predicate pushdown (skip blocks using min/max statistics) and are splittable, so queries read only the needed columns and scan less data
  • Compression: gzip (good ratio, not splittable for text), bzip2 (splittable, slow), Snappy and Zstandard (fast; common inside Parquet), LZO
  • Convert with Glue jobs (ApplyMapping, write as Parquet), Athena CTAS (format = 'PARQUET'), Firehose format conversion or EMR/Spark
  • Avoid tiny files: thousands of small objects slow listing and reads; compact them into files of roughly 128 MB to 1 GB
  • Partition the output (for example year=2026/month=11/) so queries can prune partitions
Exam tip

"Reduce Athena cost and speed up queries on CSV data in S3" → convert to Parquet (or ORC), compress, and partition.

4Connecting to and Integrating Data Sources (skills 1.2.2 and 1.2.3)

  • JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) and ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) are standard drivers that let tools and code query relational databases
  • AWS Glue connections store how to reach a data store: the JDBC URL, credentials (use AWS Secrets Manager, not clear text), and VPC, subnet and security groups; a Glue job reaches one subnet for its connections
  • Network rule: the database's security group must allow the Glue connection's security group (usually a self-referencing rule); for databases outside AWS, route through a NAT gateway (or VPN or Direct Connect)
  • Redshift and Athena also offer JDBC and ODBC drivers for BI tools; the Amazon Redshift Data API is the driverless, HTTP alternative (section 7)
  • Integrating several sources: join and union in Spark (Glue or EMR), catalog every source with crawlers so SQL engines see one schema, use federated query (Athena or Redshift) to join without copying, standardize keys, types and time zones, and de-duplicate
  • Keep raw data unchanged in a landing zone, write cleaned data to a curated zone
Exam tip

A Glue job in a VPC cannot reach the database: check security groups, subnet routing, NAT or VPC endpoints, and that credentials come from Secrets Manager.

5Optimizing Cost and Container Usage (skills 1.2.4 and 1.2.1)

Cost while processing

Lever How
Right-size Pick the smallest worker type that fits; avoid over-provisioning DPUs; use auto scaling
Flex and Spot Glue Flex execution; EMR Spot instances for task nodes; Spot for Batch and ECS
Do not run idle Transient EMR clusters, EMR Serverless, Glue (pay per run), Lambda (pay per invocation)
Read less data Columnar formats, partitioning, push-down filters, only the columns needed
Fewer, bigger files Compact small files; reduce S3 requests and task overhead
Choose the cheaper engine Lambda for tiny steps; Athena per TB scanned for occasional SQL; Redshift for steady heavy SQL
Set timeouts and limits Glue job timeout, maximum capacity, cost controls on EMR Serverless applications; AWS Budgets alerts and AWS Cost Explorer to see which jobs cost the most

Containers (Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS)

  • Run custom or long-running transforms in containers: Amazon ECS (AWS-native orchestrator) or Amazon EKS (Kubernetes); store images in Amazon ECR
  • Launch types: AWS Fargate (serverless, you set CPU and memory per task) or EC2 (you manage the instances, cheaper at steady high use)
  • Optimize for performance: set task CPU and memory to the real need, use auto scaling on queue depth or CPU, use Spot capacity for fault-tolerant batch, keep images small, and place tasks close to the data
  • AWS Batch runs batch jobs on containers with a queue and compute environment (EC2, Spot or Fargate): a fit for many independent jobs
Exam tip

"Long-running or custom-runtime transformation that does not fit Lambda or Glue" → a container on ECS or EKS (Fargate for no servers). "Thousands of batch jobs" → AWS Batch.

6Troubleshooting Failures and Slow Jobs (skill 1.2.7)

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Out of memory (driver or executor) Collecting too much to the driver, big partitions, too small a worker Larger or memory-optimized worker (G.2X, R types), more partitions, avoid collecting
One slow task Data skew: a few keys hold most rows Salt hot keys, enable adaptive query execution, repartition
Slow reads, many requests Many small files Group files, compact upstream, use columnar formats
Slow joins and shuffles Wide shuffles of large tables Broadcast the small table, filter early, partition on the join key
Cannot connect Security group, route, NAT, credentials, SSL Check the connection's VPC settings, security groups, Secrets Manager secret
Access denied IAM role of the job or Lake Formation permissions Fix the job role and S3 or Lake Formation grants
Job reprocesses old data Bookmark off, or source path changed Enable bookmarks, keep transformation_ctx stable
Lambda times out 15-minute limit, too little memory Split work, raise memory, or use Glue or Step Functions
Throttling API or service limits Backoff, more capacity, batching (Module 1)
  • Tools: CloudWatch metrics and logs (continuous logging), Glue job metrics and observability metrics, Spark UI with event logs in S3, Glue job run insights, EMR step and container logs, Athena query statistics
Exam tip

"A Spark job fails with OutOfMemoryError" → a bigger or memory-optimized worker and fewer large partitions. "One task takes hours, others seconds" → data skew.

7Data APIs: Making Data Available to Other Systems (skill 1.2.8)

  • Amazon API Gateway exposes REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs in front of Lambda, DynamoDB, Athena queries or other backends; it handles authentication (IAM, Cognito, Lambda authorizers), throttling and usage plans, caching and monitoring
  • Amazon Redshift Data API: run SQL over HTTPS with the SDK, no drivers, no persistent connections, no network setup; calls are asynchronous; authenticate with Secrets Manager, temporary IAM credentials or IAM Identity Center; a query can run up to 24 hours and results are kept 24 hours (500 MB maximum result)
  • Athena has its own API (StartQueryExecution, GetQueryResults) for programs
  • AWS Lambda function URLs give a function an HTTPS endpoint
  • Design points: paginate, cache hot results, limit result sizes, secure with IAM or tokens, and throttle to protect the backend
  • Edge and network: Amazon Route 53 gives the API a friendly DNS name, Amazon CloudFront can cache responses close to users, and AWS WAF (web exploits and bots) and AWS Shield (DDoS) protect a public API
Exam tip

"A Lambda function must run SQL on Redshift without managing connections or drivers" → Redshift Data API.

8Volume, Velocity and Variety (skill 1.2.9)

V Question it answers Effect on design
Volume How much data? Distributed processing (Spark), S3 storage, partitioning, compression
Velocity How fast does it arrive and how fast must it be used? Streaming services (Kinesis, MSK, Flink) vs batch
Variety How many shapes and sources? Schema-on-read, catalogs, formats, specialized stores
  • Structured: rows and columns with a fixed schema (relational tables, CSV with a header): RDS, Aurora, Redshift
  • Semi-structured: self-describing (JSON, XML, Avro, logs): DynamoDB, DocumentDB, S3 with Athena, OpenSearch
  • Unstructured: no schema (images, audio, video, PDFs, free text): S3, then processing with AI services or LLMs

9Using Large Language Models in Data Processing (skill 1.2.10)

  • Amazon Bedrock gives API access to foundation models; a pipeline calls it from Lambda, Glue, Step Functions or a container (InvokeModel or Converse)
  • Typical data-engineering uses: classify or tag text (the delivery notes), extract fields from documents, summarize records, clean or standardize free text, and create embeddings for vector search
  • Batch inference: submit many prompts at once (input files in S3), responses are written to S3 asynchronously: the right choice for large, non-interactive datasets; on-demand calls suit interactive or small workloads
  • Knowledge bases for Amazon Bedrock turn your documents into vector embeddings for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Module 9)
  • Amazon Kendra is intelligent enterprise search over documents; Amazon Q is a generative AI assistant that can help build and explain data integration code [Verify live]
  • Cost and safety: LLM calls cost per token, so filter first, cache repeated results and batch; keep personal data out of prompts or protect it with Bedrock Guardrails
  • Out of scope for this exam: training or tuning ML models and ML inference design
Exam tip

"Classify millions of text records overnight at the lowest cost" → Bedrock batch inference with S3 input and output.

10Exam Q&A

10.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight needs serverless ETL that cleans nightly CSV files, uses the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and requires as little infrastructure management as possible. Which service fits best?

  • AAmazon EMR on EC2 with a long-running cluster
  • BA fleet of Amazon EC2 instances running scripts
  • CAmazon Redshift stored procedures only
  • DAWS Glue Spark jobs
Show the answer

Answer: D. AWS Glue is serverless Spark ETL integrated with the Data Catalog. EMR on EC2 and EC2 fleets require cluster or instance management.

S2A team queries large CSV files in S3 with Amazon Athena and the cost and runtime are too high. What should the engineer do?

  • AConvert the data to one single large JSON file in the same prefix
  • BMove the CSV files to Amazon EBS volumes attached to Athena workers
  • CConvert the data to compressed, partitioned Apache Parquet
  • DIncrease the result retention period of the Athena workgroup
Show the answer

Answer: C. Columnar, compressed and partitioned data lets Athena read only the needed columns and partitions, so it scans less data. JSON is larger and slower to query.

S3An Apache Spark job on AWS Glue fails with OutOfMemoryError during a large aggregation. Which TWO actions are most likely to help? (Select TWO.)

  • AUse a larger or memory-optimized worker type
  • BDisable job metrics
  • CIncrease the number of partitions so each partition is smaller
  • DLower the job timeout
  • ECollect the full dataset to the driver before processing
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. More memory per worker and smaller partitions reduce memory pressure. Collecting everything to the driver makes it worse.

S4A transformation job finishes quickly for most keys but one task runs for hours because a single key holds most of the rows. What is this problem and a fix?

  • AThrottling; add retries with a longer backoff to the task
  • BA small-files problem; compress the output with gzip instead
  • CData skew; salt the hot key or enable adaptive query execution
  • DA bookmark error; reset the job bookmark and run the whole job again from the start
Show the answer

Answer: C. One key holding most rows is data skew; salting the key or enabling adaptive query execution spreads the work.

S5A Lambda function must run SQL statements on Amazon Redshift without managing database drivers, persistent connections, or VPC networking from the function. Which option should be used?

  • AA JDBC connection pool inside the function
  • BAn ODBC driver layer
  • CAmazon Kinesis Data Streams
  • DThe Amazon Redshift Data API
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Data API provides an HTTPS endpoint, uses Secrets Manager or temporary credentials, and needs no drivers or persistent connections.

S6A company must classify several million free-text delivery notes once a night at the lowest cost, and no one waits for the results. Which approach is best?

  • AUse Amazon Bedrock batch inference with prompts in S3 and results written to S3
  • BCall an on-demand foundation model once per record from a Lambda function and wait for each answer
  • CTrain a new machine learning model on EC2 and run it on every note
  • DSend the notes through Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose and classify them there
Show the answer

Answer: A. Batch inference processes many prompts asynchronously from S3 and writes results to S3, which suits large non-interactive jobs. Training a model is out of scope and unnecessary.

S7Which statement about columnar file formats is correct?

  • AThey store whole records together so that full-row reads are always fastest, even for analytics
  • BThey compress by column and let queries skip columns and blocks they do not need
  • CThey cannot be split, so one reader must process each file from the start
  • DThey are ideal for frequent updates of single records in place
Show the answer

Answer: B. Columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC compress by column and support predicate pushdown and column pruning, which reduces the data scanned.

S8A Glue job in a VPC must read from a PostgreSQL database. The job fails to connect. Which action should the engineer take FIRST?

  • ARewrite the job in Scala so that it uses a different JDBC driver
  • BCheck the Glue connection's subnet and security groups and the database's inbound rule
  • CIncrease the number of DPUs so that the connection gets more capacity
  • DChange the file format of the output to Parquet before connecting
Show the answer

Answer: B. Connection failures are usually network or credential issues: verify the connection's VPC settings, the security-group rules between the job and the database, and the secret.

Topic Key fact

EMR Managed Hadoop/Spark/Hive/Presto; EC2, EKS or Serverless; primary/core/task (Spot) nodes; transient clusters

DataBrew Visual no-code preparation

Containers ECS/EKS on Fargate or EC2; Batch for many jobs; right-size CPU and memory; Spot for fault-tolerant work

3 Vs Volume, velocity, variety; structured, semi-structured, unstructured
